# Style digest

## Violations
P0E.1 | blocker | Put only the line you expect to fail inside `try`
P0E.2 | blocker | Catch a specific exception type, with its own action; if none, an explicit suppression naming the type
P0E.3 | blocker | Catch-all only for: side channel, optional extra, batch isolation, top-level handler, rethrow with cause; name the case on the line
P0E.5 | blocker | Log inside a handler with the call that keeps the stack trace, not the one that drops it
P0F.1 | blocker | Fail fast: assert on programmer errors, validate input only at the boundary
P0F.2 | blocker | Degrade explicitly: log it and name the fallback value, never a silent `None`
P0F.3 | blocker | Do not over-protect: no defensive branch for something that fails one time in a hundred
P0F.4 | blocker | Check for empty only where the value can really be empty
P1.1 | should-fix | Nesting depth of 5 or more is a violation
P1.2 | nice | Advisory only: over 50 lines and cyclomatic complexity over 15 deserves a look
P1.3 | should-fix | A branch that assigns or returns needs an `else`, except a guard clause
P2.1 | should-fix | A base class, protocol or factory needs at least two real implementations
P2.2 | should-fix | Abstract on the third repetition, never for a hypothetical future need
P2.3 | should-fix | No config layer, plugin system or registry for a one-off need
P2.4 | should-fix | Qualify generic names: `data`, `result`, `info`, `tmp`, `manager`, `handler`, `util`
P2.5 | should-fix | Name symmetric pairs symmetrically (`start`/`stop`, `open`/`close`, `send`/`recv`)
P3.1 | nice | No comments that restate the code or the function name
P3.2 | nice | Comment the non-obvious: a decision, a pitfall, an ordering constraint
P3.3 | nice | Comments use the project's agreed language
P3.4 | nice | No debugging leftovers in a commit: stray prints, temporary TODOs, commented-out code
PRJ.1 | should-fix | house-rules only: import without execution is replay; reused IDs never exempt new execution from pre-call identity and round checks
PRJ.2 | should-fix | house-rules only: map code clauses by file conventions for category and body refs; retain valid clauses where severity omission is allowed
REL.1 | should-fix | Exempt: a cache or build output rebuilt on demand. Otherwise keep usable state until replacement is ready and validated; retain or restore it on failure
REL.3 | should-fix | Don't guard only a state file's syntax: a wrong shape takes the same fallback or named error as a parse failure, else one bad file fails every run
REL.4 | should-fix | Don't count a cap's use at the end, on success only or by opt-in: count each attempt as it starts

## Reviewer rules
R.1 | Standards come from this file, not from the reviewer
R.2 | Never rubber-stamp: if nothing is wrong, say which rule the code gets right
R.3 | Teach: every finding states the mechanism and the fix, not just the symptom
R.4 | Severity follows the family of the violated clause
R.6 | Read the surrounding code before judging a change
R.7 | Prove gates with fail/pass, reversal and per-rule mutation checks; isolate unrelated probe effects; explicitly authorize real integration effects

## Labeling

When you report findings as a JSON array, every finding object MUST carry two keys besides `file`, `line`, `summary` and `failure_scenario`:
- `"category"`: the ID of the violated clause in kebab-case (`P0E.1` -> `p0e-1`), or `"unmapped"` if no clause truly matches. Prefer `unmapped` over stretching a clause to fit.
- `"severity"`: `blocker`, `should-fix` or `nice`, the one listed for that clause under Violations.

Example: `{"file": "src/a.py", "line": 12, "summary": "...", "failure_scenario": "...", "category": "p0e-1", "severity": "blocker"}`

File one finding per defect. Mention other matching IDs in the summary instead of filing duplicates.
